keys.title: Controls
keys.subtitle: The csTimer layout: your index fingers rest on U (F = U', J = U). Clockwise and counterclockwise are separate keys. The cube starts solved and you perform the scramble yourself (or use the Scramble button); the turn speed changes each move's animation.
keys.gestureSwipe: Drag a face — the layer turns with an animated move at your turn speed and lands at exactly 90°, without following the pointer. The drag is read as if the grabbed face faced you: on the front face vertical drags turn columns R/M/L and horizontal drags rows U/E/D; on the top face horizontal drags turn F/S/B; on the side faces vertical drags turn F/S/B
keys.gestureOrbit: Drag the background — one 90° rotation per drag, with the camera locked isometric
keys.footer: Alt/Ctrl are reserved for global shortcuts. The layout matches csTimer so your muscle memory carries over.

2x2x2.cll: Corners of Last Layer — 42 cases for 2×2.

3x3x3.OLL: Orientation of Last Layer — 57 cases to orient all last layer pieces.
3x3x3.PLL: Permutation of Last Layer — 21 cases to permute the last layer pieces.
3x3x3.COLL: Corners of Last Layer — orient + permute corners when edges are oriented.
3x3x3.Winter Variation: Orient LL corners while inserting last F2L pair. 27 cases.

cube-anatomy.title: Cube anatomy
cube-anatomy.subtitle: Identify centers, edges, corners and understand piece movement
cube-anatomy.description: Learn to identify the three piece types (centers, edges, corners), understand that centers are fixed and determine face color, and recognize how layers move.
cube-anatomy.theory: A 3x3 cube has 6 fixed centers, 12 edge pieces with 2 stickers each, and 8 corner pieces with 3 stickers each. Centers define the color of each face. Understanding piece types is fundamental to all solving methods.
drills: Point to all 6 centers and name their colors
Count all 12 edges and identify their two colors
Locate all 8 corner pieces

standard-notation.title: Standard notation
standard-notation.subtitle: Read and execute R, L, U, D, F, B moves and their variants
standard-notation.description: Master the standard cube notation: clockwise (R), counter-clockwise (R'), and double (R2) turns for all six faces.
standard-notation.theory: Notation is the universal language of cubing. A letter alone = 90° clockwise, apostrophe = 90° counter-clockwise, 2 = 180°. Standard grip: white on top, green facing you. This enables reading algorithms and communicating with other cubers.
standard-notation.exampleFormula: R U R' U' (Sexy Move) — the most fundamental trigger
drills: Execute R U R' U' 6 times to return to solved state
Practice each face move looking at notation, not the cube

first-cross.title: First cross
first-cross.subtitle: Solve the white cross on the bottom face
first-cross.description: Learn to place the four white edge pieces around the white center, matching each edge's side color with its corresponding center.
first-cross.theory: The cross is the foundation of CFOP. Solving it on the bottom (not top) from day one builds good habits. Each edge must match both the bottom center AND its adjacent side center. This typically takes 6-8 moves.
drills: Practice cross on bottom 20 times without timing
Verify edge colors match both centers after each solve

first-layer-corners.title: First layer corners
first-layer-corners.subtitle: Insert white corners to complete the first layer
first-layer-corners.description: Place the four white corner pieces in their correct positions, completing the entire white face and first layer.
first-layer-corners.theory: Each corner has white plus two side colors. The corner must be placed between the corresponding side centers. The basic insertion uses R U R' or its mirror L' U' L. Avoid placing corners with white facing sideways incorrectly.
first-layer-corners.exampleFormula: R U R' — white corner insertion from right
drills: Complete first layer from scramble 10 times
Count how many moves each corner takes

middle-layer-edges.title: Middle layer edges
middle-layer-edges.subtitle: Insert the four edge pieces into the middle layer
middle-layer-edges.description: Solve the four edge pieces of the middle layer using the standard left and right insertion algorithms.
middle-layer-edges.theory: After the first layer, 4 edges remain in the middle layer. Use U R U' R' U' F' U F (right insert) or U' L' U L U F U' F' (left insert). If an edge is in the wrong slot, use the same algorithm to remove it first.
middle-layer-edges.exampleFormula: U R U' R' U' F' U F — right edge insertion
drills: Solve only the middle layer 10 times from a solved first layer
Practice recognizing edge orientation before inserting

beginner-last-layer.title: Beginner last layer
beginner-last-layer.subtitle: Complete the last layer using the 4-step beginner method
beginner-last-layer.description: Solve the yellow face and permute the last layer pieces using the beginner method: orient edges, orient corners, permute corners, permute edges.
beginner-last-layer.theory: The beginner last layer uses 4 algorithms total: F R U R' U' F' (edge orientation), R U R' U R U2 R' (Sune for corners), U R U' L' U R' U' L (corner permutation), and R U' R U R U R U' R' U' R2 (edge permutation).
beginner-last-layer.exampleFormula: F R U R' U' F' — orient yellow edges to form cross
drills: Execute each of the 4 algorithms 20 times until automatic
Complete full beginner method solves from scramble

first-complete-solve.title: First complete solve
first-complete-solve.subtitle: Solve the entire cube from any scramble without assistance
first-complete-solve.description: Complete a full solve from a scrambled cube without looking at any algorithm reference, demonstrating memory of all beginner method steps.
first-complete-solve.theory: The transition from following instructions to independent solving is the first major milestone. It requires recalling all 4-6 algorithms from memory and applying them at the right moment. Most cubers achieve this within their first week.
drills: Complete 5 full solves without any reference
Time each solve to establish your baseline

consistent-solving.title: Consistent solving
consistent-solving.subtitle: Reliably solve the cube in under 2 minutes every attempt
consistent-solving.description: Achieve consistent sub-2-minute solves with zero DNFs, demonstrating reliable recall of all beginner method steps.
consistent-solving.theory: Consistency is the hallmark of a real cuber. Being able to solve every time without failure means the algorithms are in muscle memory, not just conscious recall. This builds the foundation for all speed improvement.
drills: Complete 25 consecutive solves with 100% success rate
Record solve times and check for downward trend

cross-on-bottom.title: Cross always on bottom
cross-on-bottom.subtitle: Solve the cross directly on the bottom face without rotation
cross-on-bottom.description: Transition from solving the cross on top (then flipping) to planning and executing it directly on the bottom face.
cross-on-bottom.theory: Solving cross on bottom saves 1-2 seconds of cube rotation and lets you immediately see the F2L pieces. It requires mentally tracking pieces you can't see. Start by solving 2 edges on bottom, then complete all 4.
drills: Solve cross on bottom 50 times
Practice connecting cross edges without looking at the bottom

cross-efficiency-8.title: Cross in ≤8 moves
cross-efficiency-8.subtitle: Solve any cross in 8 moves or fewer from any scramble
cross-efficiency-8.description: Learn to find efficient cross solutions that never exceed 8 moves. The optimal cross for any scramble averages ~5.8 moves.
cross-efficiency-8.theory: Every cross can be solved in 8 moves or fewer. The key is solving edges relative to each other (not relative to centers) and doing multiple edges in one move. Advanced cross uses D-layer alignment to reduce move count.
drills: Plan cross solutions and count moves — aim for ≤7
Use cross solver tools to compare your solution with optimal

pair-preservation.title: Cross pair preservation
pair-preservation.subtitle: Preserve or position pre-existing F2L pairs while solving the cross
pair-preservation.description: Learn to track and preserve naturally formed F2L pairs during cross execution so they remain intact for instant F2L insertion.
pair-preservation.theory: During cross planning, inspect for pre-built or 1-move corner-edge pairs. Adjust your cross solution sequence to avoid separating these pairs, saving 4-5 moves during the first F2L slot without the full overhead of planning a complex XCross.
drills: Scan scrambles for pre-built pairs during inspection
Execute cross solutions while preserving at least 1 F2L pair 20 times

blind-cross.title: Blindfold cross
blind-cross.subtitle: Plan the entire cross during inspection and execute with eyes closed
blind-cross.description: Use inspection time to memorize the complete cross sequence, then execute it without looking at the bottom of the cube.
blind-cross.theory: Blind cross execution frees your eyes to look ahead for F2L pairs during cross execution. This is the first step toward lookahead. It requires visualizing all 4 edge paths during inspection and trusting your muscle memory.
drills: Plan the cross, close your eyes, execute, and check
Start with 2 edges blind, progress to all 4

cross-planning.title: Cross planning under time
cross-planning.subtitle: Plan the full cross solution within the 15-second inspection window
cross-planning.description: Consistently plan a complete, efficient cross solution within the standard WCA 15-second inspection period.
cross-planning.theory: At this level, you should identify the optimal cross face (if dual CN), plan all 4 edge placements, and rehearse the sequence mentally. Use the CsTimer inspection feature or a partner to enforce the 15s limit during practice.
drills: Set a 15s timer — plan and execute, rate your accuracy
Practice with scrambles that have 6-7 move optimal crosses

optimal-cross.title: Optimal cross selection
optimal-cross.subtitle: Choose the best cross face among multiple options for maximum efficiency
optimal-cross.description: When solving dual CN or full CN, quickly evaluate cross options on multiple faces and select the most efficient one during inspection.
optimal-cross.theory: The probability of finding a 4-move or fewer cross jumps from ~6% (single color) to ~29% (full CN). This requires rapidly scanning 2-6 faces during inspection and estimating move counts without fully planning each.
drills: Scan all available cross colors, estimate moves, pick best
Compare your choice with post-solve analysis of optimal cross

xcross-basics.title: XCross basics
xcross-basics.subtitle: Solve the cross and first F2L pair simultaneously in one sequence
xcross-basics.description: Combine cross edge placement with the first F2L pair insertion, creating a 1x2x2 block during the cross phase. This saves 4-5 moves on average.
xcross-basics.theory: An XCross leverages pre-built or nearly-built corner-edge pairs near cross edges. During cross planning, identify if any F2L pair pieces are favorably positioned. The combined sequence typically uses 7-9 moves vs 11-13 for separate cross+pair.
xcross-basics.exampleFormula: Scramble: D2 R' F B2 D2 → XCross: D2 R' U R F B2 D2
drills: Use an XCross scramble generator and solve 25 cases
Achieve XCross in 9 moves or fewer consistently

xcross-mastery.title: XCross mastery
xcross-mastery.subtitle: Find and execute XCross opportunities in 50%+ of solves
xcross-mastery.description: Recognize XCross opportunities during inspection in at least half of all scrambles, and execute them fluidly with zero hesitation.
xcross-mastery.theory: XCross mastery requires deep inspection analysis: seeing not just the cross but scanning for favorable corner-edge arrangements. This skill scales with color neutrality — more cross options = more XCross opportunities. Top cubers find XCross in 60-70% of solves.
drills: Practice 100 scrambles — identify XCross possibility in each
Time the XCross execution separately from the rest of the solve

cross-plus-two.title: Cross+2 planning
cross-plus-two.subtitle: Plan cross plus tracking of TWO F2L pairs during inspection
cross-plus-two.description: During the 15-second inspection, plan the full cross solution AND predict the landing positions of two F2L pairs for instant continuation.
cross-plus-two.theory: This is an elite-level inspection skill used by the world's best. It requires visualizing 6-8 moves of cross execution and mentally tracking 4 additional pieces simultaneously. The payoff is 2 F2L pairs solved with zero pause after the cross.
drills: Inspect for 15s, execute cross, then immediately identify pair 1 and 2
Record the number of times you correctly predict both pairs

intuitive-f2l-basics.title: Intuitive F2L transition
intuitive-f2l-basics.subtitle: Replace the beginner corner-then-edge method with paired insertions
intuitive-f2l-basics.description: Learn to pair each corner with its corresponding edge and insert them together, dramatically reducing move count vs the beginner method.
intuitive-f2l-basics.theory: F2L pairs corners and edges before insertion instead of inserting separately. This reduces the first two layers from ~8 sub-steps to 4 slots. Initially slower, it rapidly becomes faster with practice. Understanding 3 basic cases (paired, separated, corner in slot) covers most situations.
drills: Practice F2L without timing — focus on understanding piece relationships
Solve only F2L (stop after 2 layers) 25 times

f2l-case-recognition.title: F2L case recognition
f2l-case-recognition.subtitle: Instantly identify all 41 standard F2L cases and their solutions
f2l-case-recognition.description: Recognize every one of the 41 standard F2L cases without hesitation and know the optimal intuitive solution for each.
f2l-case-recognition.theory: There are 41 unique F2L cases (including mirrors). Each case can be solved intuitively by understanding how to pair pieces. Recognition speed — not execution speed — is the bottleneck for most intermediate cubers in F2L.
drills: Use F2L case trainers (J Perm, SpeedCubeDB) for all 41 cases
Drill recognition: name the case within 0.5s of seeing it

algorithmic-f2l.title: Algorithmic F2L
algorithmic-f2l.subtitle: Learn optimized algorithms for difficult F2L cases
algorithmic-f2l.description: Replace slow intuitive solutions for tough F2L cases with optimized, ergonomic algorithms that minimize regrips and rotations.
algorithmic-f2l.theory: Some F2L cases (like corner in slot, edge oriented wrong) benefit from specific algorithms. These are typically shorter and more ergonomic than the intuitive approach. Learning ~10-15 algorithmic F2L cases provides the best return on investment.
drills: Learn 3 algorithmic F2L cases per week until you've covered the hardest 15
Compare your solution vs the algorithmic one for move count

back-slot-f2l.title: Back slot insertion
back-slot-f2l.subtitle: Insert F2L pairs into back slots without cube rotation
back-slot-f2l.description: Solve F2L pairs directly into the back-left and back-right slots without rotating the cube to bring them to the front.
back-slot-f2l.theory: Back slot solving eliminates 2-4 unnecessary cube rotations per solve. It requires learning mirror solutions for cases and developing the ability to execute algorithms with pieces in non-front positions. This is a critical step toward rotationless solving.
drills: Practice 25 solves inserting all pairs only into back slots
Learn the mirror of your favorite front-slot algorithms

sledgehammer-hedgeslammer.title: Sledgehammer & hedgeslammer
sledgehammer-hedgeslammer.subtitle: Use R' F R F' and F R' F' R triggers for pair insertion and edge control
sledgehammer-hedgeslammer.description: Master the two most versatile F2L triggers. Sledgehammer (R' F R F') and Hedgeslammer (F R' F' R) for rotationless inserts and edge orientation control.
sledgehammer-hedgeslammer.theory: These 4-move triggers are fundamental building blocks. Sledgehammer inserts a pair from above while flipping edge orientation. Hedgeslammer does the mirror. Together they enable rotationless back-slot solving and edge control during the last pair.
sledgehammer-hedgeslammer.exampleFormula: R' F R F' (Sledgehammer) — inserts pair + flips 2 edges
drills: Execute each trigger 50 times focusing on fingertrick fluidity
Identify all F2L cases where these triggers apply

rotationless-f2l.title: Rotationless F2L
rotationless-f2l.subtitle: Solve all four F2L pairs without a single cube rotation
rotationless-f2l.description: Complete the entire F2L stage with zero y/y' rotations by using back-slot insertion techniques, triggers, and rotationless algorithms for all cases.
rotationless-f2l.theory: Each cube rotation costs ~0.3-0.5s. Eliminating all 4-6 typical rotations saves 1.5-3 seconds. This requires knowing solutions from every angle and using sledgehammer/hedgeslammer, wide moves, and d-moves to avoid reorienting.
drills: Complete 25 solves with a strict 0-rotation rule for F2L
For each rotation you're tempted to do, find a rotationless alternative

keyhole-technique.title: Keyhole technique
keyhole-technique.subtitle: Use empty F2L slots to insert pieces more efficiently
keyhole-technique.description: Leverage unsolved F2L slots to directly insert edge pieces in 3 moves using D-layer alignment, bypassing the standard pairing process.
keyhole-technique.theory: When a corner is already solved and the edge is in the top layer, keyhole avoids the 7-8 move standard process. Align the empty slot under the edge's target using D moves, insert in 3 moves, then restore the cross. Ideal when 1-2 corners remain unsolved.
keyhole-technique.exampleFormula: D' (align empty slot) + R U R' + D (restore cross)
drills: Solve 3 edges using only keyhole method
Identify keyhole opportunities during F2L inspection

edge-control-f2l.title: Edge orientation control
edge-control-f2l.subtitle: Manipulate top-layer edge orientation during final F2L pair insertion
edge-control-f2l.description: Choose F2L insertion variants that orient LL edges, avoiding dot OLL cases and guaranteeing favorable orientation for the last layer.
edge-control-f2l.theory: By selecting the right insertion for the 4th F2L pair (sledgehammer vs standard vs wide moves), you can orient 0, 2, or 4 LL edges. This guarantees a cross OLL and eliminates the slowest 8 OLL cases (dots).
edge-control-f2l.exampleFormula: Instead of R U R', use R' F R F' to flip 2 edges
drills: Complete 50 solves targeting zero dot OLLs via edge control
For each last slot, identify which insertion gives best edge orientation

zbls-set.title: ZBLS (last slot edge control)
zbls-set.subtitle: Orient all LL edges during final F2L pair insertion regardless of pair state
zbls-set.description: Master ZBLS (Zborowski-Bruchem Last Slot) to force all top-layer edges to orient during the last F2L slot, setting up 1-look ZBLL.
zbls-set.theory: While basic edge control uses Sledgehammer for simple cases, ZBLS covers all last-slot scenarios (split pair, edge in slot, corner in slot). Orienting edges during the final F2L slot guarantees an oriented LL cross, unlocking 1-look ZBLL every solve.
drills: Learn 10 essential ZBLS cases for common unjoined last-slot setups
Combine ZBLS practice with ZBLL T/U set execution

multislotting.title: Multi-Slotting
multislotting.subtitle: Solve two adjacent F2L pairs in one unified sequence
multislotting.description: Combine the insertion of two F2L pairs into a single fluid sequence without intermediate pauses or recognition gaps.
multislotting.theory: Multi-slotting leverages the movement of one pair to set up the pieces of the next pair. A 2-pair multislot typically saves 3-4 moves vs separate solutions. It requires tracking both slot states simultaneously and recognizing dual-pair patterns.
multislotting.exampleFormula: R U2 R' U R U' R' + L' U L (2-pair multislot)
drills: Practice 2-pair prediction: identify what the cube looks like after pair 1
Learn 5-10 common multislotting patterns

pseudo-slotting.title: Pseudo-Slotting
pseudo-slotting.subtitle: Form F2L pairs relative to a temporarily offset cross alignment
pseudo-slotting.description: Solve F2L pairs assuming the D-layer is rotated off-alignment, resolving all pairs simultaneously with a final D or D2 alignment move.
pseudo-slotting.theory: Pseudo-slotting unlocks cases that look terrible under standard orientation. By temporarily offsetting the cross alignment (D or D'), 'bad' pairs become easy. At the end, one D/D2 move aligns everything. Used extensively by elite cubers for difficult cases.
pseudo-slotting.exampleFormula: D (offset) + U R U' R' + D' (alignment)
drills: Practice pseudo-F2L pair recognition under active D-rotations
Learn to identify when offsetting would help a difficult case

two-look-oll.title: 2-look OLL
two-look-oll.subtitle: Orient the last layer in 2 steps: edges then corners (10 algorithms)
two-look-oll.description: Replace the beginner OLL with the 2-look system: 3 edge orientation cases plus 7 corner orientation cases for a reliable 2-step solution.
two-look-oll.theory: 2-look OLL reduces OLL from 57 to 10 algorithms. Step 1 orients edges (3 cases: line, L-shape, dot). Step 2 orients corners (7 cases: Sune, Anti-Sune, etc.). This is the standard intermediate approach and sufficient for sub-20 solving.
two-look-oll.exampleFormula: F R U R' U' F' → orient edges (line case)
drills: Learn all 10 algorithms in one week (1-2 per day)
Use OLL trainer to randomize all 10 cases

two-look-pll.title: 2-look PLL
two-look-pll.subtitle: Permute the last layer in 2 steps: corners then edges (6 algorithms)
two-look-pll.description: Replace the beginner PLL with the 2-look system: 2 corner permutation cases plus 4 edge permutation cases.
two-look-pll.theory: 2-look PLL reduces PLL from 21 to 6 algorithms. Step 1 permutes corners (A-perm or E-perm). Step 2 permutes edges (Ua, Ub, H, Z). Combined with 2-look OLL, this gives a 4-step last layer — sufficient for sub-25.
two-look-pll.exampleFormula: R U R' U' R' F R2 U' R' U' R U R' F' → T-Perm (corner swap)
drills: Learn all 6 algorithms with correct fingertricks
Practice recognition: identify the PLL case in under 1 second

full-pll.title: Full PLL
full-pll.subtitle: Learn all 21 PLL algorithms for 1-step last layer permutation
full-pll.description: Memorize and execute all 21 PLL algorithms with consistent sub-2.5s execution each, enabling 1-step permutation of the last layer.
full-pll.theory: Full PLL is the highest-value algorithm set for intermediate cubers. 21 algorithms unlock 1-step PLL. Focus on ergonomic algorithms and fingertricks from day one — bad finger habits are hard to unlearn. Target: sub-2s per PLL.
full-pll.exampleFormula: R U R' U' R' F R2 U' R' U' R U R' F' — T-Perm
drills: PLL Time Attack: execute all 21 PLLs back-to-back, target sub-45s
Learn 3 new PLLs per day for one week

two-sided-pll-recog.title: 2-Sided PLL Recognition
two-sided-pll-recog.subtitle: Identify any PLL case by seeing only two adjacent faces
two-sided-pll-recog.description: Determine the exact PLL case from only two visible sides, eliminating the need to rotate the cube to see all faces for recognition.
two-sided-pll-recog.theory: This saves ~0.5s per solve by avoiding recognition rotations. Each PLL has unique 2-sided patterns based on color bars, headlights, and opposites. Most cubers learn this naturally after full PLL, but deliberate study accelerates mastery.
drills: Cover two faces and identify the PLL from the visible two
Use 2-sided PLL recognition trainers (J Perm, SpeedCubeDB)

auf-prediction.title: AUF Prediction & Execution
auf-prediction.subtitle: Predict and execute Adjust Upper Face moves during LL recognition and execution
auf-prediction.description: Anticipate the final U, U', or U2 alignment move during PLL recognition and execute it seamlessly without post-alg hesitation.
auf-prediction.theory: AUF (Adjust Upper Face) pauses cost 0.2s–0.4s per solve. By tracking key sticker bars during PLL recognition and algorithm execution, elite cubers determine the required AUF move before the algorithm finishes, executing it as part of the last move trigger.
drills: Practice PLL execution ending immediately with predicted AUF
Drill 2-sided recognition and call out AUF before starting the alg

full-oll.title: Full OLL
full-oll.subtitle: Learn all 57 OLL algorithms for 1-step last layer orientation
full-oll.description: Memorize and execute all 57 OLL algorithms with consistent sub-1.5s execution, enabling 1-step orientation every solve.
full-oll.theory: 57 OLL cases are grouped by shape: dot (8), line (4), L-shape (8), cross (7), P-shape (4), T-shape (2), W-shape (2), square (2), fish (4), bolt (6), awkward (4), and all corners oriented (7). Learn grouped by shape for easier memorization.
drills: Learn OLL in groups of 4-8, starting with the most common shapes
Use OLL trainer to drill all 57 cases randomized

oll-recognition-speed.title: OLL recognition speed
oll-recognition-speed.subtitle: Identify OLL cases in under 0.5 seconds from any angle
oll-recognition-speed.description: Achieve near-instant OLL recognition by internalizing shape patterns rather than counting oriented pieces or stickers.
oll-recognition-speed.theory: Fast OLL recognizers see the overall shape (fish, knight move, lightning bolt) instantly. This is developed through high-volume exposure. Top cubers recognize OLL in 0.2-0.3s — faster than conscious thought.
drills: Flash card drills: show OLL for 0.3s and name it
Recognition-only practice: identify 100 OLLs without executing them

coll-set.title: COLL set
coll-set.subtitle: Solve corner orientation AND permutation in one algorithm (40 cases)
coll-set.description: When the LL cross is already formed, use COLL to solve corners in one step, leaving only edge PLLs (Ua, Ub, H, Z) or a PLL skip.
coll-set.theory: COLL is 40 algorithms grouped by corner orientation (H, Pi, U, T, L, Sune, Anti-sune). After COLL, only 4 fast edge PLLs remain. COLL is also a prerequisite and stepping stone to ZBLL. PLL skip occurs ~1/6 of the time.
coll-set.exampleFormula: F R U R' U' R U R' U' F' — COLL H case
drills: Learn COLL by orientation group (start with H and Pi — 8 cases)
Drill recognition by headlight colors (front and side)

winter-variation.title: Winter variation
winter-variation.subtitle: Insert final F2L pair while orienting all LL corners (27 cases)
winter-variation.description: When the LL cross is formed and the last F2L pair is joined, use WV to orient corners during insertion, achieving an OLL skip.
winter-variation.theory: Winter Variation covers 27 cases where the last F2L pair is joined in the top layer and LL edges are oriented. Executing WV orients corners during insertion, skipping OLL entirely and going straight to PLL.
winter-variation.exampleFormula: R U2 R' U' R U' R' — WV Case 1 (corner facing right)
drills: Learn WV grouped by corner orientation (3 main groups)
Practice recognizing when WV is applicable during last slot

ollcp-basics.title: OLLCP basics
ollcp-basics.subtitle: Orient LL while permuting corners to force favorable PLL cases
ollcp-basics.description: Use specific OLL variants that also permute corners, leaving only edge PLLs or achieving a PLL skip. Master key OLLCP subsets for common OLL shapes.
ollcp-basics.theory: OLLCP extends OLL by recognizing corner permutation before execution. By choosing an OLL that also permutes corners correctly, you eliminate corner PLLs. Learning OLLCP for the 7 cross-OLL cases is the highest-value starting point.
drills: Learn OLLCP for cross OLL cases first (highest frequency)
Practice corner permutation recognition before OLL execution

vls-basics.title: VLS (Valk Last Slot)
vls-basics.subtitle: Insert last F2L slot and solve OLL simultaneously regardless of edge state
vls-basics.description: A superset of Winter Variation covering cases where LL edges are NOT oriented. Insert the last pair while solving OLL in one step.
vls-basics.theory: VLS extends WV to unoriented edge cases. It covers ~216 cases total — typically only a subset is learned. Most useful when the last slot has a joined pair and you want to force OLL completion during insertion.
vls-basics.exampleFormula: F R U R' U' F' + R U R' — VLS for specific edge orientation
drills: Start with VLS cases that appear most frequently in your solves
Use VLS recognition flashcards grouped by edge orientation

zbll-t-u.title: ZBLL T & U sets
zbll-t-u.subtitle: Learn the T and U sets of ZBLL — 1-look LL when edges are oriented (144 cases)
zbll-t-u.description: Solve the entire last layer in ONE algorithm when edges are oriented. Master the T and U subsets first — the most common and ergonomic ZBLL cases.
zbll-t-u.theory: ZBLL removes the PLL step entirely when LL edges are oriented. T and U sets (72 cases each) are the most common and have the best algorithms. This is where elite cubers invest their algorithm learning time for maximum ROI.
zbll-t-u.exampleFormula: R U2 R' U' R U' R' U2 R U R' U R U2 R' — ZBLL U case
drills: Learn ZBLL T-set first (72 cases) over 2-3 months
Use ZBLL recognition trainers for Tran-style recognition

full-zbll.title: Full ZBLL mastery
full-zbll.subtitle: Complete 1-step last layer resolution — all 472 ZBLL cases
full-zbll.description: Master the complete ZBLL set: all 472 cases across T, U, L, H, Pi, Sune, and Anti-sune groups for 1-look last layer in every edge-oriented scenario.
full-zbll.theory: Full ZBLL is the ultimate last layer achievement. 472 cases organized into 7 groups. Combined with ZBLS/edge control to guarantee oriented edges, this enables consistent sub-0.8s last layer. Only a handful of cubers worldwide have truly mastered full ZBLL.
drills: Complete L, H, and Pi sets after T and U (total ~472 cases)
ZBLL time attack: execute random ZBLL cases at sub-1.2s each

basic-lookahead.title: Basic lookahead
basic-lookahead.subtitle: Look for the next F2L pair while solving the current one
basic-lookahead.description: Train your eyes to scan for the next corner-edge pair while your hands execute the current insertion, eliminating the pause between F2L slots.
basic-lookahead.theory: Lookahead is the single most important skill for breaking through speed plateaus. The brain has ~0.5-1s of 'free' processing during any F2L insertion — use it to find the next pair. Slow down execution to give your eyes time to look ahead.
drills: Slow-turning practice: solve at 50% speed, focus only on piece tracking
Metronome practice: turn one move per beat at 60 BPM, never pause

f2l-lookahead.title: F2L lookahead flow
f2l-lookahead.subtitle: Maintain continuous piece awareness through all four F2L slots
f2l-lookahead.description: Develop the ability to track multiple F2L pieces simultaneously and seamlessly transition from one slot to the next with zero pause.
f2l-lookahead.theory: Top cubers 'know' which pair they will solve next before finishing the current one. This requires training peripheral vision and pattern anticipation. Start by always knowing your NEXT pair before your current pair is inserted.
drills: Pair prediction: before inserting, say aloud which pair you'll solve next
Solve F2L pairs in any order based on what you see first

cross-f2l-transition.title: Cross→F2L transition
cross-f2l-transition.subtitle: Track the first F2L pair during cross execution
cross-f2l-transition.description: During the final cross moves, locate and begin tracking the first F2L pair so you can start it immediately after cross completion.
cross-f2l-transition.theory: The cross-to-F2L transition is the most common pause point. If your cross is planned in inspection, your eyes are free during execution to find pair #1. The goal: 0.0s pause between the last cross move and first F2L move.
drills: Practice cross→F2L exclusively: solve cross, then immediately insert pair 1
Use a metronome at 3 TPS, never pause between cross and F2L

metronome-pacing.title: Metronome pacing
metronome-pacing.subtitle: Solve at a consistent, externally-paced rhythm to eliminate pauses
metronome-pacing.description: Use a metronome to enforce steady turning speed, training your eyes to track pieces at a fixed pace without rushing or pausing.
metronome-pacing.theory: A metronome at 60-180 BPM forces consistent TPS. Start slow (60 BPM = 1 TPS) and increase gradually. When you can solve at 120 BPM without pauses, your lookahead can handle 2 TPS. This trains your brain to process visual information at speed.
drills: Start at 60 BPM, increase by 10 BPM when you can solve pause-free
Target: 180 BPM (3 TPS) with zero pauses in F2L

continuous-lookahead.title: Continuous lookahead
continuous-lookahead.subtitle: Maintain unbroken piece tracking from cross through PLL
continuous-lookahead.description: Achieve a state where your eyes are always one step ahead of your hands throughout the entire solve, with no visual pauses.
continuous-lookahead.theory: Continuous lookahead means your eyes never stop scanning. During F2L pair 3, you're already tracking pair 4. During OLL execution, you're already identifying the PLL case. This flow state is what separates 15-second cubers from 10-second cubers.
drills: Solve at 70% max speed — prioritize smoothness over TPS
Video record solves and count pause frames between steps

predictive-tracking.title: Predictive tracking
predictive-tracking.subtitle: Anticipate where pieces will end up after your current moves
predictive-tracking.description: Mentally simulate how your current moves affect piece positions, predicting their final locations before the sequence completes.
predictive-tracking.theory: Predictive tracking eliminates the 'search' phase after each insertion. By understanding how your algorithm moves pieces, you know where to look next before you finish. This requires deep familiarity with how each F2L case affects the cube.
drills: Before inserting a pair, predict exactly where pair 2 pieces will be
Practice tracking a specific edge through multiple F2L insertions

zero-pause-flow.title: Zero-pause flow
zero-pause-flow.subtitle: Solve with absolutely zero pauses — every move flows into the next
zero-pause-flow.description: Enter a flow state where the solve is one continuous motion without any recognition pauses, hesitations, or breaks in rhythm.
zero-pause-flow.theory: Zero-pause solving is the hallmark of elite speedcubers. Every move is connected. Recognition, decision, and execution form one seamless loop. This requires all algorithms in muscle memory, all recognition patterns subconscious, and full lookahead mastery.
drills: Record solves and check for ANY frame without a turn
Target: max 0.3s pause at any point in the solve

subconscious-recognition.title: Subconscious Recognition
subconscious-recognition.subtitle: Recognize cases instantly without conscious thought — pure pattern response
subconscious-recognition.description: Process OLL, PLL, and F2L cases at a subconscious level, where your hands begin executing before you consciously 'know' what the case is.
subconscious-recognition.theory: At the highest level, recognition bypasses conscious thought. Pattern → algorithm mapping becomes a direct neural pathway. This is achieved through thousands of repetitions. Your hands 'know' the algorithm before your conscious mind names the case.
drills: Speed recognition drills at 2x normal pace
Practice naming cases while executing them to verify subconscious knowledge

basic-u-flicks.title: Basic U flicks
basic-u-flicks.subtitle: Execute U and U' moves with index finger pushes and pulls
basic-u-flicks.description: Learn the fundamental index finger techniques: right index push for U, left index pull for U', replacing whole-hand wrist turns.
basic-u-flicks.theory: U flicks are the most common moves in cubing. Right index pushes the UFR corner forward for U. Left index pulls the UBL corner toward you for U'. These are faster and more precise than wrist turns and are the foundation of all fingertricks.
drills: Execute (U U') x 20 focusing on finger movement, not wrist
Practice trigger R U R' U' repeatedly for 30 seconds

r-moves-proper.title: R-move technique
r-moves-proper.subtitle: Execute R and R' with proper wrist and finger technique
r-moves-proper.description: Master R moves using the right hand with minimal regripping, and learn the proper grip that allows fluid R and U combination triggers.
r-moves-proper.theory: R is executed by pulling the right layer toward you with the right hand. R' pushes it away. The key is keeping the cube stable with the left hand while the right executes. Learn to hold the cube so R and U moves can flow together without regripping.
drills: Practice R U R' U' trigger 50 times, maintaining grip stability
Execute all PLL U-perms focusing on R-U flow

f-move-ergonomics.title: F & F' move ergonomics
f-move-ergonomics.subtitle: Execute F and F' moves using index finger pinches and thumb flicks without regripping
f-move-ergonomics.description: Master index finger pinches for F and thumb flicks for F' to execute frontal face turns seamlessly from standard home grip.
f-move-ergonomics.theory: Wrist-heavy F moves cause regrips and slow down algorithms like T-Perm, Sledgehammer, and OLLs. Pushing F with the right index finger and flicking F' with the right thumb allows rapid execution while keeping hands fixed in home grip.
drills: Execute F R U R' U' F' 30 times using index pinch for F and thumb flick for F'
Practice T-Perm paying attention to seamless F/F' transitions

double-flicks-u2.title: Double flicks (U2)
double-flicks-u2.subtitle: Execute U2 in one fluid motion using index-middle finger combo
double-flicks-u2.description: Master the U2 double flick: right index followed by right middle finger in one seamless motion, achieving U2 in half the time of two separate U moves.
double-flicks-u2.theory: The U2 double flick is a core speed technique. Right index pushes, then right middle finger immediately follows through. The key is keeping both fingers close to the U layer and maintaining momentum. Also learn the left-hand mirror for ambidextrous solving.
drills: Execute U2 double flicks 100 times each hand
Practice algs with many U2s (H-Perm, Z-Perm) at speed

d-moves-ring.title: D-move ring technique
d-moves-ring.subtitle: Execute D and D' moves with ring fingers for cross and F2L efficiency
d-moves-ring.description: Use ring fingers to execute D-layer moves without regripping, essential for efficient cross execution and keyhole F2L techniques.
d-moves-ring.theory: D moves are critical for cross and keyhole. Right ring finger pushes DFR corner for D, left ring finger pushes DFL for D'. Practice these in cross sequences: a good cross often alternates R, U, and D moves seamlessly.
drills: Execute D and D' with ring fingers 50 times, minimize hand shift
Practice cross sequences incorporating D moves without pauses

m-slice-basics.title: M-slice technique
m-slice-basics.subtitle: Execute M, M', and M2 for advanced algs and Roux
m-slice-basics.description: Learn proper M-slice execution: M' with ring/middle finger push from back, M with pull from front, and M2 double flick.
m-slice-basics.theory: M moves follow the L direction: M' goes the same direction as L', M goes with L. For M', push the BD edge forward with your ring or middle finger from behind. M pulls the UF edge toward you. Essential for H-Perm, Z-Perm, and Roux LSE.
drills: Execute H-Perm (M2 U M2 U2 M2 U M2) 25 times focusing on M2 flicks
Practice M' U and M U' triggers in isolation

advanced-finger-tricks.title: Advanced finger tricks
advanced-finger-tricks.subtitle: Master wide moves (r,l,f), S-slice, and pinch moves
advanced-finger-tricks.description: Expand your physical vocabulary to include wide turns, S/E-slice moves, and compound techniques that reduce move counts in advanced algorithms.
advanced-finger-tricks.theory: Wide moves (r = R + M') are essential for rotationless OLL. S-slice moves appear in advanced F2L. Pinch moves (thumb+index gripping a layer) enable fast F and B moves. Each new physical technique unlocks faster execution of advanced algorithms.
drills: Practice r U R' U' r' F R F' (wide OLL trigger)
Learn S-move technique for ZBLL and advanced F2L algorithms

regrip-minimization.title: Regrip minimization
regrip-minimization.subtitle: Reduce hand repositioning to near-zero throughout the entire solve
regrip-minimization.description: Eliminate unnecessary regrips by choosing algorithms that flow naturally from the ending position of the previous step.
regrip-minimization.theory: Every regrip costs ~0.2-0.3s. A solve with 10 regrips loses 2-3 seconds. Choose algorithms that end in positions compatible with the next step. Use the home grip consistently. Plan algorithm transitions so your hands are always ready.
drills: Record solves and count regrips — target: ≤2 per solve
Audit your algorithm set: replace algorithms that cause regrips

peak-tps-execution.title: Peak TPS execution
peak-tps-execution.subtitle: Achieve and maintain 10+ TPS on known algorithms with full accuracy
peak-tps-execution.description: Push your physical turning speed to elite levels (10-12+ TPS) on algorithms while maintaining lockup-free accuracy and fluid transitions.
peak-tps-execution.theory: TPS naturally increases with practice but plateaus without deliberate speed training. Focus on 'burst TPS' during PLL execution and steady-state TPS during F2L. The balance is speed vs lockups — faster is only better if you don't lock up.
drills: PLL Time Attack targeting sub-35s for all 21
TPS burst drills: execute T-Perm as fast as possible, verify accuracy

inspection-basics.title: Inspection basics
inspection-basics.subtitle: Use the 15-second WCA inspection to plan the cross before starting
inspection-basics.description: Learn to use inspection time productively: locate cross pieces, plan a basic cross solution, and position hands before starting the timer.
inspection-basics.theory: Inspection is not just 'looking at the cube' — it's active planning. Find all four cross edges, plan their sequence, and rehearse mentally. Even planning 2-3 edges is better than starting blind. Build the habit of using every second of inspection.
drills: Use a 15s countdown — plan what you can, then execute
Start with planning 2 cross edges, progress to all 4

cross-planning-inspect.title: Full cross during inspection
cross-planning-inspect.subtitle: Plan the complete 4-edge cross solution within 15 seconds every solve
cross-planning-inspect.description: Consistently plan all four cross edge placements during inspection, including move sequence and final positions of cross edges.
cross-planning-inspect.theory: This is the baseline inspection skill for sub-25 solving. Identify each cross edge's path, calculate the sequence, and visualize the final cross state. The brain can hold 6-8 moves in working memory easily — a full cross plan fits within this limit.
drills: Use unlimited inspection initially, then reduce to 15s
After solving cross, verify all edges match both centers

full-inspection-15s.title: 15-second inspection mastery
full-inspection-15s.subtitle: Maximize every second of inspection: plan cross and spot F2L opportunities
full-inspection-15s.description: Structure your 15 seconds: 5s for cross planning, 5s for cross rehearsal, 5s for F2L piece spotting — extracting maximum value from inspection.
full-inspection-15s.theory: Elite cubers have a structured inspection routine: (1) locate cross pieces on preferred face, (2) plan sequence, (3) mentally rehearse, (4) identify first F2L pair pieces. This deliberate structure prevents panic and maximizes pre-solve preparation.
drills: Practice with a partner enforcing strict 15s inspection
After inspection, rate yourself: did you find pair 1 pieces?

cross-one-inspect.title: Cross+1 inspection
cross-one-inspect.subtitle: Plan the cross AND predict the location of the first F2L pair during inspection
cross-one-inspect.description: During the 15-second inspection, plan the full cross AND identify or predict where the first F2L pair pieces will end up after cross execution.
cross-one-inspect.theory: Cross+1 is the single highest-impact inspection skill for breaking sub-15. By tracking the corner and edge of pair 1 through your cross solution, you eliminate the post-cross pause entirely. This requires visualizing the cube state after cross completion.
drills: Cross+1 drill: execute cross, immediately solve pair 1 without pause
Track a specific piece through cross — predict its final location

pair-prediction.title: Multi-pair prediction
pair-prediction.subtitle: Predict how F2L pairs change during cross and between slots
pair-prediction.description: During inspection and throughout the solve, mentally track how piece positions evolve with each move, anticipating F2L pairs multiple steps ahead.
pair-prediction.theory: Multi-pair prediction is the bridge to elite solving. By understanding how cross moves affect F2L pieces, you can spot emerging pairs before they fully form. This requires deep cube awareness — knowing where each tracked piece goes after every move.
drills: After planning cross, predict which corner-edge combinations will be near each other
Track all 8 F2L pieces through cross execution (name their positions)

multi-solution-compare.title: Multi-solution comparison
multi-solution-compare.subtitle: Evaluate multiple cross/F2L strategies during inspection and pick the best
multi-solution-compare.description: In 15 seconds, mentally compare 2-3 cross approaches and select the one with the best F2L follow-up potential, not just the shortest cross.
multi-solution-compare.theory: The shortest cross is not always the best. An 8-move cross with perfect F2L setup beats a 5-move cross with terrible follow-up. At the master level, inspection involves strategic choice: which face? XCross possible? Best pair 1 accessibility?
drills: For each scramble, plan 2 different crosses, compare quality
Time the first 15 moves for each cross choice, compare results

full-solve-planning.title: Full solve architecture
full-solve-planning.subtitle: Mentally outline the entire solve structure during inspection
full-solve-planning.description: Develop a high-level solve strategy during inspection: cross plan, F2L slot solving order, potential XCross/multislot opportunities, and transition awareness.
full-solve-planning.theory: At the elite level, inspection isn't just about cross+1 — it's about solve architecture. Which slots look easy? Which pair should be last? Is WV applicable? This strategic overview prevents mid-solve indecision and ensures optimal slot ordering.
drills: During inspection, name the order you'll solve F2L slots
After solve, compare planned vs actual slot order

single-cross-mastery.title: Single Cross Mastery
single-cross-mastery.subtitle: Achieve consistent, efficient solves on one cross color before expanding
single-cross-mastery.description: Master your primary cross color (typically white) to the point where cross planning and F2L recognition are automatic and effortless.
single-cross-mastery.theory: Before expanding to other colors, your primary color should be deeply ingrained — you should see F2L pairs instantly and plan crosses in seconds. This ensures you have a 'home base' to return to when learning new colors feels frustrating.
drills: Achieve consistent sub-30 solves on white cross before starting CN
Ensure cross planning on white takes ≤12 seconds in inspection

dual-color-neutrality.title: Dual Color Neutrality
dual-color-neutrality.subtitle: Solve on both white and yellow cross with equal proficiency
dual-color-neutrality.description: Extend your solving ability to the opposite cross color (yellow if you started on white), maintaining the same lookahead and recognition speed.
dual-color-neutrality.theory: Dual CN (white + yellow) is the most practical step toward full CN. F2L colors are identical (just inverted), so recognition patterns transfer easily. The cross on the second color will be slow at first — expect ~100 solves before comfort.
drills: Complete 100 solves exclusively on yellow cross
Compare yellow vs white solve times — target: within 10%

opposite-color-training.title: Opposite Color Training
opposite-color-training.subtitle: Add red/orange and blue/green cross pairs systematically by dedicated practice blocks
opposite-color-training.description: Methodically add new cross colors one pair at a time, building recognition patterns for non-primary colors through dedicated practice blocks.
opposite-color-training.theory: The most effective CN training method: dedicate 1-2 weeks per new color pair (red+orange first, then blue+green). Solve 50+ solves per day on the new color. The CNY method: Color-Neutral-Yellow, alternating new colors with yellow solves to maintain dual CN.
drills: Week 1-2: red cross only (100 solves total)
Week 3-4: orange, Week 5-6: blue, Week 7-8: green

full-color-neutrality.title: Full Color Neutrality
full-color-neutrality.subtitle: Solve on any of the six faces with zero hesitation or speed penalty
full-color-neutrality.description: Achieve complete color neutrality: inspect and choose the best cross among all six faces without any speed difference between colors.
full-color-neutrality.theory: Full CN increases the probability of finding a ≤4-move cross from ~6% to ~29%. It requires rewiring F2L recognition to be color-relative rather than color-absolute. At full mastery, you won't remember which color you started on after the solve.
drills: Random cross color sessions: let a die choose your cross color
Target: all 6 colors within 5% of each other in average time

subconscious-cn.title: Subconscious Color Neutrality
subconscious-cn.subtitle: Choose the optimal cross color automatically during inspection without conscious deliberation
subconscious-cn.description: Your brain automatically evaluates all six faces during inspection and selects the best option without you consciously 'trying' each color.
subconscious-cn.theory: At this level, CN is fully internalized. Your eyes scan all faces in 2-3 seconds and your brain registers the best option. You no longer see 'colors' — you see relative block positions and cross edge arrangements. This frees cognitive resources for deeper inspection.
drills: Time your color selection: pick the best cross in under 3 seconds
After solve, try to recall which color you used — if you can't, you've internalized CN

cube-anatomy-hardware.title: Cube Hardware 101
cube-anatomy-hardware.subtitle: Understand cube components: core, screws, springs, pieces, and how they interact
cube-anatomy-hardware.description: Learn the physical construction of a speedcube: core mechanism, center pieces with screws/springs, edge pieces with torpedoes, and corner pieces with stalks.
cube-anatomy-hardware.theory: A modern speedcube has a spherical core with 6 screws+springs for tensioning, 12 edge pieces with anti-pop torpedoes, and 8 corner pieces. Understanding how these interact helps with setup and maintenance decisions.
drills: Disassemble and reassemble your cube to understand its structure
Identify all components and their functions

basic-lubrication.title: Basic Lubrication
basic-lubrication.subtitle: Apply lube correctly to improve speed, smoothness, and cube lifespan
basic-lubrication.description: Learn to clean and lubricate your cube: disassemble, apply lube to tracks and core, reassemble, and break in properly.
basic-lubrication.theory: Lubrication reduces friction between pieces. Thin/fast lubes go on piece tracks for speed. Thick lubes go in the core for stability and control. Apply 2-4 drops, spread evenly, and do 50+ solves to break in. Over-lubing makes cubes gummy.
drills: Complete your first clean+lube cycle following a video guide
Test cube feel before and after to understand lube effect

tensioning-basics.title: Tensioning Basics
tensioning-basics.subtitle: Adjust screw tension and spring compression for optimal cube feel
tensioning-basics.description: Understand how screw depth and spring compression affect stability, corner cutting, and speed. Find your personal optimal tension.
tensioning-basics.theory: Tighter screws = more stable but slower, less corner cutting. Looser = faster but more lockups and pops. Spring compression controls resistance. Most modern cubes have dual-adjustment: set screw depth for overall tension, adjust compression for spring feel.
drills: Experiment with 3 tension levels: loose, medium, tight — feel the difference
Find the tightest setting that still allows 45° corner cutting

magnet-adjustment.title: Magnet Adjustment
magnet-adjustment.subtitle: Configure magnet strength for your turning style and speed
magnet-adjustment.description: Adjust or swap magnets to match your turning force. Stronger magnets = more stability and snap, weaker = more fluidity with less resistance.
magnet-adjustment.theory: Magnets provide tactile feedback and auto-alignment. Core magnets (corner-to-core) add stability without slowing individual layer turns. Edge-corner magnets help with alignment. Adjustable systems let you fine-tune the magnetic 'click' to your preference.
drills: Try all magnet settings on your adjustable cube
Note solve times and feel at each setting to find your sweet spot

cube-selection.title: Cube Selection Strategy
cube-selection.subtitle: Choose the right cube for your skill level, style, and goals
cube-selection.description: Understand the speedcube market: budget, mid-range, and flagship cubes. Match cube characteristics to your solving style and level.
cube-selection.theory: Beginners: any modern magnetic budget cube ($10-20). Intermediate: dual-adjustment cubes ($25-40). Advanced: flagship cubes with core magnets and customization ($40-80). Key factors: turning feel (crunchy vs buttery), size (54-56mm), and weight.
drills: Research the top 5 cubes used in recent WCA competitions
If possible, try a friend's cube to compare feels

custom-cube-setup.title: Custom Cube Setup
custom-cube-setup.subtitle: Create a personalized cube setup matching your exact preferences
custom-cube-setup.description: Combine lube selection, tension optimization, and magnet configuration into a personalized setup that maximizes YOUR turning style.
custom-cube-setup.theory: Every cuber's setup is unique. Fast turners prefer tighter tensions with light lube. Precise solvers prefer stronger magnets. The perfect setup is iterative: adjust one variable at a time, test with 50+ solves, then tweak again.
drills: Document your current setup (lube type, tensions, magnet strength)
Adjust one variable, solve 50 times, record feel and times

maintenance-optimization.title: Maintenance & Optimization
maintenance-optimization.subtitle: Regular cleaning, re-lubrication, and wear monitoring for peak performance
maintenance-optimization.description: Establish a maintenance routine: cleaning schedule, lube reapplication timing, spring replacement, and monitoring cube wear over thousands of solves.
maintenance-optimization.theory: Cubes degrade gradually: lube dries out, springs weaken, plastic wears. A maintained cube should be cleaned every 500-1000 solves and re-lubed. Springs lose tension after ~10k solves. Regular maintenance prevents gradual speed loss.
drills: Create a maintenance log: track solves since last clean/lube
Learn to identify when your cube needs lubrication by feel

nerves-management.title: Nerves Management
nerves-management.subtitle: Control competition anxiety and maintain composure under pressure
nerves-management.description: Develop techniques to manage nervousness: breathing exercises, positive self-talk, and reframing anxiety as excitement.
nerves-management.theory: Competition nerves are universal — even world champions feel them. The difference is how they're managed. Deep breathing (4-7-8 pattern) activates the parasympathetic nervous system. Reframing 'I'm nervous' as 'I'm excited' changes the physiological response.
drills: Practice 4-7-8 breathing before timed solves
Simulate competition pressure: have someone watch you solve

pre-solve-routine.title: Pre-Solve Routine
pre-solve-routine.subtitle: Develop a consistent ritual before each solve to center focus and trigger flow
pre-solve-routine.description: Create a repeatable pre-solve ritual: deep breath, hand warmup, visualization, and intention setting — performed identically every solve.
pre-solve-routine.theory: A pre-solve routine is a psychological anchor. It signals your brain 'we're about to solve now' and triggers the optimal mental state. Most elite cubers have a specific sequence: inspect hands, deep breath, pick up cube, start inspection — always the same.
drills: Design a 10-second pre-solve routine and use it for 50 solves
Evaluate if consistency improved with the routine

bad-solve-recovery.title: Bad Solve Recovery
bad-solve-recovery.subtitle: Reset mentally after a poor solve and prevent one bad result from cascading
bad-solve-recovery.description: Develop the resilience to immediately reset after a bad solve, treating each attempt as independent and preventing negative momentum.
bad-solve-recovery.theory: The 'reset skill' is crucial in Ao5 format where one bad solve can cascade. Physical reset: put cube down, shake hands out, deep breath. Mental reset: treat the bad solve as data, not failure. The next solve is a fresh opportunity with zero connection to the last.
drills: After a bad solve, time your reset: can you be mentally ready in 10 seconds?
Practice with deliberate bad scrambles to train reset response

competition-strategy.title: Competition Strategy
competition-strategy.subtitle: Plan approach: safe vs risky solves, round management, and pacing
competition-strategy.description: Develop strategic thinking for WCA competitions: when to play it safe (qualification rounds) and when to push for speed (finals).
competition-strategy.theory: Competition strategy varies by round. Qualification rounds: prioritize consistency and avoid DNFs — safe crosses, comfortable algorithms. Finals: push limits with aggressive lookahead and faster execution. Know the cut-off times and plan accordingly.
drills: Simulate competition format at home: 5 solves, Ao5 scoring
Practice 'safe mode' (95% speed) and 'push mode' (100% speed) separately

focus-techniques.title: Deep Focus Techniques
focus-techniques.subtitle: Achieve sustained concentration during long practice sessions and competitions
focus-techniques.description: Train your ability to maintain high-quality focus for extended periods using concentration techniques from sports psychology.
focus-techniques.theory: Focus is a trainable skill. The Pomodoro technique (25 min focus, 5 min break) works for cubing practice. During competitions, 'tunnel vision' focus — blocking out crowd noise, other competitors, and external stimuli — preserves mental energy between solves.
drills: Practice with deliberate distractions (music, conversation, noise)
25-minute focused sessions with 5-minute breaks

flow-state.title: Competition Flow State
flow-state.subtitle: Enter the optimal performance state where solving feels effortless and automatic
flow-state.description: Achieve the flow state during competition: complete absorption in the solve, loss of self-consciousness, and effortless automatic execution.
flow-state.theory: Flow state (Csikszentmihalyi) occurs when challenge perfectly matches skill. In cubing, flow means hands execute while conscious mind observes. Entry conditions: clear goals (the solve), immediate feedback (piece movement), and focused attention.
drills: Practice 'observer mode': let hands solve while you watch passively
Identify your personal flow triggers (music, silence, specific warmup)

elite-composure.title: Elite Composure
elite-composure.subtitle: Maintain world-class calm, confidence, and mental clarity in any competitive scenario
elite-composure.description: Develop the unshakeable mental foundation of a world-class competitor: calm under all conditions, confident without arrogance, focused without tension.
elite-composure.theory: Elite composure is built through exposure and reflection. Every competition, every failure, every success is data for mental growth. The goal: perform at your practice level (or better) regardless of stakes, audience, opponent, or prior results.
drills: Compete regularly — composure only develops through real pressure
After each competition, journal what went well mentally and what to improve

session-structure.title: Training Session Structure
session-structure.subtitle: Design effective practice sessions with clear goals rather than mindless solving
session-structure.description: Learn to structure practice time: warmup, focused drills, timed solves, cooldown — replacing 'just solving' with deliberate, goal-oriented sessions.
session-structure.theory: Mindless solving is the #1 reason cubers plateau. A structured session: 5min warmup (slow solves), 15min focused drill (your weakest area), 20min timed solves tracking progress, 5min cooldown. Each session has one specific improvement goal.
drills: Plan your next 5 practice sessions with specific goals
Track what you practiced and whether you improved

physical-ergonomics.title: Physical Ergonomics & Wrist Care
physical-ergonomics.subtitle: Practice hand stretches, posture, and strain prevention for safe high-TPS cubing
physical-ergonomics.description: Maintain hand, wrist, and forearm health through regular warming up, stretching, and ergonomic posture to prevent strain injuries like RSI.
physical-ergonomics.theory: High-volume speedcubing at 8-12+ TPS puts intense physical strain on finger tendons and wrist flexors. Incorporating 2-minute forearm stretches, wrist rotations, and proper seating posture prevents repetitive strain injuries (RSI) and long-term fatigue.
drills: Perform wrist and finger stretches before every high-volume practice session
Take 5-minute active rest breaks every 30 minutes of speed solving

deliberate-practice.title: Deliberate Practice
deliberate-practice.subtitle: Target specific weaknesses with focused drills rather than general solving
deliberate-practice.description: Implement deliberate practice: identify your weakest skill, isolate it, drill it exclusively, and measure improvement before moving on.
deliberate-practice.theory: Deliberate practice (Ericsson) is the science of skill acquisition. Identify your bottleneck (slow cross, poor F2L lookahead, PLL recognition), create isolated practice for that exact skill, drill with immediate feedback, and only move on when measurable improvement occurs.
drills: Identify your #1 weakness using split timing analysis
Dedicate 3 sessions exclusively to that weakness

algorithm-drilling.title: Algorithm Drilling System
algorithm-drilling.subtitle: Use systematic drilling and spaced repetition to master algorithms permanently
algorithm-drilling.description: Apply spaced repetition principles to algorithm learning: drill new algorithms daily at first, then progressively space reviews as mastery increases.
algorithm-drilling.theory: Spaced repetition optimizes long-term algorithm retention. New alg: practice 20x immediately, then 10x after 1 hour, 5x next day, then every 3 days until automatic. Use algorithm trainers (J Perm, SpeedCubeDB) that track per-algorithm speed.
drills: Create a spaced repetition schedule for your current algorithm learning set
Track execution time for each algorithm over 2 weeks

weakness-analysis.title: Weakness Analysis
weakness-analysis.subtitle: Use split timing and solve reconstruction to identify your exact bottlenecks
weakness-analysis.description: Analyze your solves scientifically: measure time per phase, compare against benchmarks for your target level, and identify the biggest gap.
weakness-analysis.theory: Raw solve times hide the real story. Split analysis reveals: is your cross 3s when it should be 2s? Is F2L recognition 60% of your time? Use CubeForge's analysis tools or CsTimer's multi-phase timing to get per-phase data. Fix your biggest gap first.
drills: Complete 25 solves with phase timing, identify worst phase
Compare your splits against benchmarks for your target level

split-analysis.title: Split Analysis & Benchmarking
split-analysis.subtitle: Compare your phase splits against target-level benchmarks to guide improvement
split-analysis.description: Use standardized split benchmarks (cross, F2L, OLL, PLL times) for each skill level to identify which phase is holding you back.
split-analysis.theory: Benchmark splits: Sub-20: Cross≤3s, F2L≤10s, OLL≤3s, PLL≤4s. Sub-15: Cross≤2.5s, F2L≤7.5s, OLL≤2.5s, PLL≤2.5s. Sub-10: Cross≤1.8s, F2L≤5s, OLL≤1.5s, PLL≤1.7s. Compare your splits, focus on the phase furthest from target.
drills: Record splits for 50 solves and create a phase-by-phase average
Set a target split for each phase based on your next level goal

smart-training-planning.title: Smart Training Planning
smart-training-planning.subtitle: Create data-driven weekly training plans based on your split analysis
smart-training-planning.description: Design weekly training plans that allocate practice time proportionally to your weaknesses, with built-in progress tracking and plan adjustment.
smart-training-planning.theory: A smart training plan allocates time based on need, not preference. If cross is your weakness (30% above benchmark) and OLL is fine, spend 40% of practice on cross, 30% on F2L, 20% on PLL, 10% on OLL. Re-assess weekly and rebalance.
drills: Create a 4-week training plan based on your current split analysis
Re-assess splits after 4 weeks and adjust the plan

periodization.title: Training Periodization
periodization.subtitle: Structure long-term training in cycles: build, peak, recover, compete
periodization.description: Apply athletic periodization principles to speedcubing: structured cycles of skill building, speed peaking, tapering, and competition performance.
periodization.theory: Periodization prevents burnout and maximizes competition performance. Build phase (3-4 weeks): learn new techniques and algorithms. Peak phase (2 weeks): maximize TPS and flow. Taper (1 week pre-comp): reduce volume, maintain quality. Compete: perform, then recover (1 week light practice).
drills: Plan a 6-week periodization cycle leading to a target date
Track volume, intensity, and performance throughout the cycle

roux-first-block.title: Roux First Block
roux-first-block.subtitle: Build a 1x2x3 block on the left side efficiently and intuitively
roux-first-block.description: Learn to construct the first 1x2x3 block (left side) using intuitive block building, typically in 7-10 moves, without relying on algorithms.
roux-first-block.theory: The first block is Roux's foundation. Build the 1x2x2 (square) first, then add the remaining 1x1x2 pair. Plan during inspection — identify a 2x2 square opportunity and expand. This builds spatial reasoning that benefits ALL methods.
drills: Practice first block only (stop after FB) 50 times
Target: first block in ≤10 moves, planned during inspection

roux-second-block.title: Roux Second Block
roux-second-block.subtitle: Build the 1x2x3 block on the right side without breaking FB
roux-second-block.description: Construct the second 1x2x3 block on the right side using only R, r, M, and U moves, preserving the completed first block.
roux-second-block.theory: After FB, the cube is restricted to R, r, M, and U moves (no L, F, B). This constraint makes SB faster but requires different pair-building techniques. The square-first approach mirrors FB: build a 1x2x2, then add the final pair.
drills: Practice second block starting from a solved first block
Target: second block in ≤15 moves using only R/r/M/U

roux-cmll.title: Roux CMLL
roux-cmll.subtitle: Solve all corners in one algorithm — 42 cases (ignoring M-slice)
roux-cmll.description: Learn all 42 CMLL algorithms to solve the last layer corners in one step, ignoring the M-slice which is solved in LSE.
roux-cmll.theory: CMLL solves corners while ignoring the M-slice and U-layer edges. 42 cases (7 orientation groups × 6 permutation cases). Recognition is by top-face color pattern and side stickers. CMLL uses R and U moves primarily — fast and ergonomic.
drills: Learn CMLL grouped by orientation (start H and Pi — 8 cases)
CMLL time attack: execute all 42 sub-50s

roux-lse-basics.title: LSE Basics
roux-lse-basics.subtitle: Solve Last Six Edges: orientation, UL/UR placement, and final permutation
roux-lse-basics.description: Master the LSE phase in 3 sub-steps: edge orientation, UL+UR edge placement, and M-slice permutation.
roux-lse-basics.theory: LSE uses only M and U moves. Step 1: orient all 6 edges (recognize bad edges on U/D faces using arrow rule). Step 2: place UL/UR edges on the bottom. Step 3: permute the remaining 4 M-slice edges (4 cases: Ua, Ub, H, Z equivalents).
drills: Practice LSE edge orientation recognition — identify bad edges in under 2s
Drill the 4 final M-slice permutation cases

roux-lse-advanced.title: Advanced LSE
roux-lse-advanced.subtitle: Optimize LSE with advanced techniques: EOLR and efficient UL/UR placement
roux-lse-advanced.description: Apply EOLR (Edge Orientation + Left/Right placement combined) and other advanced LSE techniques to reduce move count and eliminate pauses.
roux-lse-advanced.theory: Advanced LSE combines EO and UL/UR placement into fewer moves. EOLR places UL/UR edges while orienting — saving 3-5 moves. Advanced solvers also use misoriented centers and BU recognition for the final permutation.
drills: Learn EOLR for the 6 most common edge orientation patterns
Practice LSE with BU (back-up) edge recognition

roux-eolr.title: EOLR Mastery
roux-eolr.subtitle: Combine edge orientation with LR edge placement in one fluid step
roux-eolr.description: Full EOLR integration: orient all edges and place UL/UR edges simultaneously, reducing LSE from 3 sub-steps to effectively 2.
roux-eolr.theory: EOLR is the biggest advancement in Roux LSE. Instead of orient edges → place LR → permute M-slice, EOLR combines the first two. There are ~30 EOLR cases based on misoriented edge count and LR edge positions.
drills: Learn EOLR cases grouped by edge orientation count
Practice EOLR→4c (M-slice permutation) as one continuous flow

roux-non-matching.title: Non-Matching Blocks
roux-non-matching.subtitle: Build blocks regardless of center color alignment, resolving at the end
roux-non-matching.description: Use non-matching blocks (NMB) to exploit favorable piece positions even when centers don't align, fixing the offset at the end of the solve.
roux-non-matching.theory: NMB allows building blocks relative to a 'wrong' center, solving pieces that would be difficult with standard alignment. The offset is corrected later in the solve. This technique is especially powerful in Roux and provides flexibility similar to pseudo-slotting in CFOP.
drills: Practice first block with offset centers (e.g., build on red when blue is correct)
Learn to track the offset and resolve it during LSE

roux-full-mastery.title: Roux Full Mastery
roux-full-mastery.subtitle: Complete Roux proficiency at expert level with sub-10 capability
roux-full-mastery.description: Achieve full Roux mastery: efficient blocks (~25 moves), instant CMLL recognition, advanced EOLR, and zero-pause LSE — capable of sub-8 solves.
roux-full-mastery.theory: Roux at the highest level rivals CFOP. The method excels in low move count (averaging 45-50 moves vs CFOP's 55-60) and high TPS potential in LSE. Mastery requires ~5000+ dedicated Roux solves and full integration of all advanced techniques.
drills: Complete 1000 Roux solves tracking block efficiency and LSE speed
Target: first block in ≤7 moves, second block ≤12, CMLL sub-1.5s, LSE sub-2s

zz-eoline.title: EOLine
zz-eoline.subtitle: Orient all 12 edges and place DF/DB edges in one step during inspection
zz-eoline.description: Learn to orient all 12 edges and place the DF and DB edges simultaneously — the signature first step of the ZZ method.
zz-eoline.theory: EOLine is ZZ's defining step. Count bad edges (edges that can't be solved using only R, L, U, D). An even number of bad edges is orientable. Place DF and DB while fixing bad edges. After EOLine, the cube is solvable using only R, U, and L moves.
drills: Practice counting bad edges — identify all within 5 seconds
Plan EOLine during inspection — target: 8-10 moves

zz-eocross.title: EOCross
zz-eocross.subtitle: Orient edges while solving the full cross (not just the line) for better F2L
zz-eocross.description: Transition from EOLine to EOCross: orient all edges AND solve the full cross (DF, DB, DL, DR edges) in one step for better lookahead.
zz-eocross.theory: EOCross is more moves than EOLine but sets up a much better F2L stage. With a full cross solved and all edges oriented, F2L becomes rotationless by definition. Most modern ZZ solvers prefer EOCross for its ergonomic advantages.
drills: Plan EOCross during inspection — target: 12-14 moves
Compare EOLine vs EOCross solves to find your preference

zz-f2l.title: ZZ F2L
zz-f2l.subtitle: Rotationless F2L using only R, U, and L moves with all edges oriented
zz-f2l.description: Solve F2L pairs using only R, U, L moves — no cube rotations needed since all edges are pre-oriented. Focus on block building efficiency.
zz-f2l.theory: ZZ F2L's main advantage: ZERO rotations. All pairs are solved in the front 180° hemisphere. Pairs can go into RF, LF, RB, or LB slots with equal ease. This trains rotationless solving skills that transfer directly to CFOP.
drills: Practice ZZ F2L only (stop after F2L) — target: sub-8s
Compare move count with your CFOP F2L to see efficiency gains

zz-coll-epll.title: ZZ COLL+EPLL
zz-coll-epll.subtitle: Use COLL for corner control and EPLL for fast edge permutation
zz-coll-epll.description: Apply COLL (40 cases) to solve corners after F2L, then use EPLL (4 cases: Ua, Ub, H, Z) to finish — the standard expert ZZ last layer.
zz-coll-epll.theory: Since ZZ orients all edges in the first step, the LL cross is always formed after F2L. This makes COLL the natural choice: solve corners in one step, leaving only the 4 fast edge PLLs. This is more efficient than standard OLL+PLL.
drills: Combine COLL recognition with EPLL execution into one flow
Target: COLL+EPLL in under 3.5s total

zz-zbll.title: ZZ to ZBLL
zz-zbll.subtitle: Full ZBLL integration — the ultimate ZZ last layer since edges are always oriented
zz-zbll.description: Leverage ZZ's guaranteed edge orientation to use ZBLL for 1-look last layer — solving OLL and PLL simultaneously in every solve.
zz-zbll.theory: ZZ + ZBLL is a natural pairing: ZZ guarantees oriented LL edges, which is exactly ZBLL's prerequisite. This means EVERY solve ends in a 1-look last layer. Combined with rotationless F2L, this is one of the most efficient solving systems possible.
drills: Only ZBLL cases applicable (edges already oriented — the full set is usable)
Practice ZZ specifically with ZBLL for T and U subsets first

zz-ct.title: ZZ-CT
zz-ct.subtitle: ZZ with Corner Twisty — insert last pair solving CP for 2GLL finish
zz-ct.description: Apply the ZZ-CT variant: use TSLE (tran-style last edge) during final pair insertion, then 2GLL for 2-gen last layer.
zz-ct.theory: ZZ-CT is an alternative to ZBLL. TSLE inserts the last F2L edge while orienting corners (~100 cases). Then 2GLL solves the rest using only R and U moves. This trades ZBLL's algorithm count for a 2-step system with better ergonomics.
drills: Learn TSLE for the most common last-slot edge positions
Practice 2GLL recognition (2-gen PLL and ZBLL variants)

zz-full-mastery.title: ZZ Full Mastery
zz-full-mastery.subtitle: Complete ZZ proficiency with competition-ready sub-10 capability
zz-full-mastery.description: Achieve full ZZ mastery: efficient EOCross, optimized rotationless F2L, and rapid ZBLL or CT last layer — capable of sub-8 solves.
zz-full-mastery.theory: ZZ at the elite level combines the best of all worlds: rotationless solving, 1-look last layer, and low move counts. Fewer top solvers use ZZ than CFOP, but those who master it achieve remarkable efficiency. Average move count: 45-50.
drills: Complete 1000 ZZ solves tracking EOCross efficiency and LL speed
Target: EOCross in ≤12 moves, F2L sub-6s, last layer sub-2s

bld-old-pochmann.title: Old Pochmann Method
bld-old-pochmann.subtitle: Solve edges and corners one piece at a time using the classic BLD method
bld-old-pochmann.description: Learn the Old Pochmann method: use a fixed buffer piece and swap individual edges/corners using T-Perm and Y-Perm — the entry point to blindfolded solving.
bld-old-pochmann.theory: OP uses a buffer piece (UR for edges, UBR for corners) and swaps it with the target piece using setup moves + T-Perm (edges) or modified Y-Perm (corners). Each piece is solved individually. This method teaches the fundamentals of BLD piece tracing.
bld-old-pochmann.exampleFormula: T-Perm: R U R' U' R' F R2 U' R' U' R U R' F' — edge swap
drills: Practice T-Perm and Y-Perm until they're automatic with eyes closed
Trace edge cycles on a solved cube with your eyes open first

bld-memo-basics.title: BLD Memo Basics
bld-memo-basics.subtitle: Learn Speffz letter scheme and basic memorization for edges and corners
bld-memo-basics.description: Master the Speffz lettering scheme and create a basic memo system: assign letters to stickers, trace piece cycles, and create memorable words/images.
bld-memo-basics.theory: Speffz assigns one letter to each sticker (24 edge stickers = A-X, 24 corner stickers = A-X). Tracing cycles: start at buffer, follow the piece that belongs there, continue until back at buffer. Convert letter pairs into memorable images or words.
drills: Practice tracing edge cycles on a solved cube (no memo needed)
Create your letter pair image list for all 576 combinations

bld-m2-op.title: M2 for Edges
bld-m2-op.subtitle: Upgrade edge solving from Old Pochmann to M2 — faster, fewer moves per edge
bld-m2-op.description: Replace Old Pochmann edges with the M2 method: use the DF buffer and M2 move to swap pieces, with special algorithms for M-slice targets.
bld-m2-op.theory: M2 is significantly faster than OP for edges. Each edge is solved with M2 + setup moves (1-3 moves typically). M-slice targets (FU, BD, BU) require special handling. Combined with OP corners, M2/OP is the standard intermediate BLD method.
drills: Practice M2 edge execution without memo until it's fluid
Learn the special M-slice target algorithms (FU, BD, BU cases)

bld-letter-pairs.title: Letter Pair Images
bld-letter-pairs.subtitle: Build a complete letter pair image system for rapid and reliable memorization
bld-letter-pairs.description: Develop a personal letter pair image system: a unique, vivid image for every two-letter combination (AA, AB, AC... XX) for fast memo encoding.
bld-letter-pairs.theory: Letter pair images are the standard BLD memo technique. Each pair of letters becomes one mental image (e.g., QK = Quack, MB = Mobile). Images are placed in a memory palace (Roman room) or linked in a story. A good image system enables sub-30s memo.
drills: Create images for all 576 letter pairs over 2-4 weeks
Practice memo-only: memorize, wait 5 minutes, recall without solving

bld-audio-loops.title: Audio Loop Memo
bld-audio-loops.subtitle: Use rhythmic audio repetition for short-term edge memo during execution
bld-audio-loops.description: Apply audio loop memorization for edges: convert letter sequences into rhythmic sounds you repeat internally during corner execution.
bld-audio-loops.theory: Audio memo is for short-term recall (edges, executed second). Convert letter string into a rhythmic sound loop (e.g., 'KA-JE-PO-SU-TA' with rhythm). Repeating this internally during corner execution keeps it in phonological working memory. Enables sub-15s edge memo.
